en: Third Chapter.
By the merit of their subjects, kings—whose affection is fixed upon their own realms and who are accompanied by many devoted people—arise like auspicious seasons. (3.1)

To do good for the virtuous, to behold the goddess Lakṣmī, to travel through the sky, and to hear the life-story of the great-souled ones—the mind of one who is curious about these things [longs for them]. (3.2)
Then, on one occasion, when the clouds had thinned,
when the *kādamba* birds warbled, causing anxiety to the *cātaka* birds, and when the peacocks’ pride was stolen by their loathing for the frogs—
When the sky was like a polished sword-blade, and the sun was shining brightly, serving as a guest-house for the entire caravan of travelers on the path of the swans.
When the moon was bright,
the clusters of young stars were appearing,
and the bow of Indra was beginning to fade.

When the lightning-garland was fading away, when [the world] was hostile to the sleep of Damodara, and when Indra’s clouds— light with their swirling mists— were rendered fruitless in the waters that possessed the hue of molten lapis lazuli;
With the *nīpa* trees closing their petals,
the *kuṭaja* trees devoid of blossoms,
and the *kandalī* lilies lacking buds;
O you who possess tender lotuses, who have blue lotuses dripping with honey,
and who delight with white water-lilies!
When the night was cooled by *śephālikā* flowers, fragrant with *yūthikā*,
and the ten directions were made bright white by blooming water-lilies;

When the breeze was greyed by the pollen of the *saptacchada* trees; when the unseasonable twilight was being dispelled by the lovely *bandhūka* flowers and *svabhāvaka* blossoms; and when the horses had been sprinkled with water for purification.
When the wild female elephants were intoxicated with pride, the bulls were wasting away,
the circles of mud were diminishing,
and the riverbanks were sprouting young sandbanks;
When the śyāmāka grain has ripened and dried, when the pollen of priyaṅgu blossoms has been produced, and when the skin of the trapusa fruit has become hard;
When the arrows of the flower-bowed god [Kāma] began to bloom and the season of autumn commenced, Bāṇa returned once more to that Brahmin settlement to see his kinsmen from the presence of the king.
His relatives, highly gratified by the extraordinary honor bestowed upon him by the monarch, went forth praising him as they emerged.
And in due course, he was saluting some, being saluted by others, and being kissed on the head by still others.
Smelling some on the head,
being embraced by some, and embracing others;
Being favored with blessings by others,
bestowing favors upon others,
and situated among many kinsmen, he rejoiced exceedingly.
When his elders had taken their seats, he occupied a seat brought by his bewildered attendants;
and as they paid him honor with worship and other marks of respect, he rejoiced exceedingly.
With a delighted mind, he questioned them all: "I trust you have been well during these many days?"

Is the sacrificial rite being performed without hindrance, satisfying the assembly of twice-born with its correct execution; or are the fire-eating gods consuming the oblations accompanied by complete and unerring mantras;
or are the young students studying at the proper time?
Is there the daily, uninterrupted recitation of the Vedas? Is that same long-standing application to the study of sacrificial science still maintained?
Are those very circles of exegesis present, which display such earnest devotion day after day through their mutual rivalry in grammar?
"Is that very assembly of authoritative scholars, who have long since abandoned all other duties, still present?
Or is that same extraordinary passion for Mīmāṃsā, which has dulled one's interest in other sciences, still there?
And are those conversations on poetry, which rain down the nectar of fresh elegant sayings, still occurring?"
Then they said to him:

"Father, for those who delight in contentment, whose diversion is the constant study of knowledge, and whose only companions are the sacrificial fires—how little need have they for worldly happiness? For the King of the Earth, whose body is as long as the serpent king who supports the entire world, protects the earth."
"In every respect we are indeed happy, especially now that you, having cast off all indolence, stand by the side of the Supreme Lord and preside over the cane seat;
and all the various rites appropriate for Brahmins are being performed according to our ability, according to our means, and at the proper times."

With such conversations as these, along with accounts of the army camp, recollections of games from his childhood past, and stories of his ancestors, he remained for a long time with them, his mind delighted;
and rising at midday, he performed the customary duties as they were observed.
And when he had finished eating, all his kinsmen gathered around him.

In the meantime, he was wearing two garments made of fine *dukūla* silk, as pale as the side-glances of a peacock; at the conclusion of his bath, he had applied a sectarian mark (*tilaka*) with clay from a sacred ford and yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), both offered by his wife, while the hair on his head was smoothed with oil and *āmalaka*.
He was resplendent with a dense floral garland that reached up to touch his topknot;
the luster of the red dye on his lips was pure from the frequent use of betel-leaf; and the beauty of his eyes was enhanced by the application of single-stick collyrium.
Having recently eaten,
wearing a modest and noble dress,
the reciter of books, Sudṛṣṭi, arrived.
He sat down on a seat not far away.

Having remained there for a moment as if, he placed the book—though its binding thread had been removed at that time, it was nevertheless encircled by the rays of his nails as if by soft lotus fibers—upon a mechanical device of arrows and sticks set before him.

Then, having lifted up the leaf marked with the sign for the break in the morning recitation, he settled himself in the place offered by two bamboo flutes in the form of a bee and a pigeon perched close together behind him.

Taking up a small door-leaf made of a few leaves, he recited the Purāṇa proclaimed by Pavana with a melody that captivated the minds of the listeners through its sweet modulations— as if washing away the soot-stained letters with the luster of his teeth, as if honoring the text with offerings of white flowers, and as if with the sounds of the anklets of Sarasvatī placed near his mouth.

And while Sudṛṣṭi was thus reciting that which was filled with songs pleasing to the ear, the bard Sūcībāṇa, standing not far away, followed the melodic drone with his own voice, sweet and high-pitched, and sang this pair of Āryā verses:
"Though it is sung by a sage, it is exceedingly vast; though it pervades the world, it is purifying; though it is ancient, it appears to me as if it were inseparable from the *Harṣacarita*. (3.3)
This song, which issues from Śrīkaṇṭha, is consistent with its lineage, possesses clear articulation, and is weighty through its adherence to the path of Bharata; it is like the kingdom of Harṣa.
Having heard that, Bāṇa’s four sons— whose forms were purified by the study of the Vedas like the lotus-faces of the Grandfather (Brahmā),
and whose mouths were charming in the application of conciliation like the [four] means of policy—
[were led by] Gaṇapati.
Adhipati, Tārāpati, and Śyāmala were brothers, the sons of his paternal uncle.
Their conduct was serene,
they had mastered the sacred texts,
and they had performed the ritual placement of the teacher's feet.

They were proponents of right reasoning, masters through the practice of accumulating merit, and possessed of refined speech; like those in the world, they were experts in grammar and conversant with the histories of all the ancient royal sages,
their souls purified by the Mahābhārata.
They were great scholars and eminent poets who had mastered the entirety of history.
They were curious about the life stories of great beings,
for whom the taste of hearing well-spoken words was an elixir, and who were free from craving.
Foremost in age, speech, fame, asceticism, assembly, majesty, and physical form as well as in the Yajurveda,
they had already made their vow and were desirous of speaking.
With the hollows of their cheeks whitened by the nectar of their smiles,

they gazed upon one another’s faces. Then, the youngest among them— named Śyāmala, whose eyes were as long as lotus petals, who was dear to Bāṇa and the master even of his very life— having been given a sign by them, spoke with affection, bathing the quarters with the moonlight of his teeth.

With his moon-like face, he spoke: "Dear Bāṇa, Purūravas, the king of the twice-born, committed the abduction of his preceptor’s wife; through his greed for a Brahmin’s wealth, he was deprived of his beloved life.
Nahuṣa, out of desire for another’s wife, became a great serpent."
Yayāti fell [from heaven] after having taken the hand of a Brahmin woman;
Sudyumna became entirely female;
and Somaka’s mercilessness in slaying living beings was famous throughout the world.

Māndhātṛ, due to his addiction to hunting, went to the netherworld along with his sons and grandsons; Purukutsa, even while performing austerities, committed a despicable act by violating Mekalakandakā;
and Kuvalayāśva, because of his attachment to the world of serpents, did not abandon even the daughter of Aśvatara.
Pṛthu, the first of men, subdued the earth;
even during the time of Nṛga’s existence as a lizard, a confusion of castes was observed;
and by Saudāsa, the earth—protected by Naraka—was thrown into turmoil.
Kali overcame Nala, whose heart was no longer under his own control; Sāgara fell into despondency regarding the daughter of his friend;
and Daśaratha met his death through the madness of longing for Rāma.
Kārtavīrya met his end through the excessive oppression of cows and Brahmins;
Marutta, despite having performed sacrifices with much gold, was not highly esteemed by the gods and the twice-born;
and Śantanu, due to his excessive addiction, lamented alone in the forest, separated from his army.
Like a fish cast into the middle of a forest, Pāṇḍu, overwhelmed by the essence of passion, abandoned his life;
and Yudhiṣṭhira, his heart despondent with fear of his elders, renounced truth at the head of battle.
Thus, there is no kingship free from blemish except for that of the God of gods, Harṣa, who enjoys all the continents and is immortal.
Indeed, many wonders are heard concerning this place.
For instance: here, the moving mountains with their wings spread were rendered motionless by Bali;
here, Prajāpati established his seat for a moment upon the circle of the serpent Śeṣa.
Here, Puruṣottama, having crushed the King of Sindhu, made Lakṣmī his own; here, Balarāma, having released the coils of the mountain, liberated the great serpent;
and here, the Prince was consecrated by the Lord.
Here, the power of the Lord was proclaimed by him who felled his enemies with a single blow; here, the valor of Narasiṃha was manifested by him who slaughtered his enemies with his own hands;
and here, the hand of Durgā, whose home is the snowy mountain, was taken by the Supreme Lord.
Here, the Lord of the World appointed the guardians of the quarters at the cardinal points,
and the entire treasury of the world was distributed among the Brahmins;
such great undertakings as these are seen, just as they were in the first Kṛta Age.

Therefore, we desire to hear from the beginning, following the chronological succession of his ancestors, the life-story of this one whose name is well-cherished, that great mass of merit. A very long time has passed for us who are eager to listen.
For the virtues of the great attract the minds of even the base, just as magnets draw iron, however dry and hard it may be.
How much more so for others, whose natures are naturally tender and soft?
Who would not have curiosity regarding his life story, which is like a second *Mahābhārata*? Please tell us.
"Let this lineage of Bhṛgu become even more pure through the hearing of these virtuous deeds of the royal sages," having said this,
he became silent.
Bāṇa, however, laughed and said, "Noble sir!"
What you have said is not consistent with reason;
I perceive your curiosity to be like an unattainable desire.
Generally, those who thirst for their own interests are devoid of any discrimination between what is possible and what is impossible.
I believe that even the minds of the great lose their discernment when they are enamored with the virtues of others and deluded by the impetuous passion for hearing stories of beloved people.
Let the Noble One observe: where is the heart of this young Brahmin, which is the size of an atom;
and where is the life-story of Your Majesty, which pervades the entire universe from Brahma down to a blade of grass?
Where are these few words describing the virtues of the perfections, and where are those qualities that transcend all number?
This is beyond the reach even of the Omniscient One.
It is beyond the reach even of Vācaspati,
and an excessive burden even for Sarasvatī; how much more so for one such as I?
Indeed, who could possibly describe his life-story in its entirety even in a hundred human lifetimes?
But if you have curiosity regarding a single portion of it, we are ready.
Where will this tongue of mine, which has acquired but a tiny fragment of a few syllables, find any utility?
You are the listeners;
the *Harṣacarita* is being described.
What else?

The Blessed One, radiant with a mass of matted locks consisting of the tawny rays of the sun hanging low in the sky, is sinking into the great lake of the Samantapañcaka like the venerable Bhārgava Rāma; tomorrow, when the veil of twilight’s crimson glow has vanished, I shall announce it.
And they all replied, "So be it.
Before long, having risen, he went to the Śoṇa river to perform his twilight devotions.
Then, as the day closed like a bud, its soft glow fading upon the cheeks of the Mālava women who were blooming with the intoxication of wine;

As the sun, devouring the darkness, hung low as if out of grief for the closing of the lotus beds; and as the darkness rushed through the sky like the buffalo of Yama, following the path of the sun’s chariot horses; and as the bark garments, hanging from the thatched roofs of the house-dwellers’ huts, were gradually gathered in along with the fragments of red sunlight; Please note: The text provided is a single, continuous Sanskrit passage describing the onset of twilight. Here it is: As the sun, which devours the darkness, hung low as if out of grief for the closing of the lotus beds; and as the darkness rushed through the sky like the buffalo of Yama, following the path of the sun's chariot horses; and as the bark garments, hanging from the thatched roofs of the house-dwellers' huts, were gradually gathered in along with the fragments of red sunlight;
While the smoke from the sacrificial fires, which steals away the sins of the Kali age, was filling the sky; while the sacrificers were observing their vows according to the rules of Manu;
and while the wives were wandering about, restless at the hour for the ritual distribution of food.

While the green and dark-green tufts of śyāmāka and śāli rice were being scattered about, while the tawny cows used for oblations had been milked, while the sacrificial fire was being fed with offerings, and while the young students—
seated upon purified mats, wearing matted hair and black antelope skins— were engaged in silent recitation;

While the assembly of yogis meditated as they occupied the Brahmā-throne, while the endless disciples ran about to the sound of clapping hands, while the dull-witted elderly Vedic scholars, with their consent, were chanting out the strings of verses from crumbling manuscripts, and while the host of fat, lecherous youths was intently scrutinizing the sky for the star known as Jyotis; (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the "star known as Jyotis," but the translation reflects the full context available.)
When the onset of evening arrived, he returned to his residence and sat down with his affectionate kinsmen, remaining in that very same conversation.
Having passed the first watch of the night, he retired to the bed prepared for him in the palace of Gaṇapati.
But for all the others, whose eyes were closed yet who had not fallen asleep—waiting like beds of lotuses for the rising of the sun—the night somehow came to an end through their intense curiosity.
Then, having awakened during the fourth watch of the night, that same bard recited two verses:
"Stretching out his hind legs, bending his back and extending his body high,
with his neck curved and his mouth pressed against his chest, he shakes his mane, grey with dust."
Desiring a mouthful of grass, the horse, its muzzle constantly flickering, makes a low sound as it rises from its bed and scratches the earth with its hoof. // 3.5 //
With his back arched and his neck bent close to his mouth, the horse—
his ears pressed tight against his head— scratches the itch of sleep with his flickering mane, which is white as frost and tossing sideways as he strikes it.
With his hoof, he struck the corner of his eye, where a tiny speck of dust had become lodged against the tips of his eyelashes.
Bāṇa, having heard that, cast off his sleep, arose, washed his face, and performed the worship of the divine Twilight; then, when the divine Sun had risen, he took his betel and remained right there.
In the meantime, all his kinsmen arrived and sat down surrounding him.

He too, having understood their intention through their previous gestures, began to recount the *Harṣacarita* before them: "Listen—there exists a dwelling place for those who have performed meritorious deeds, like the abode of Indra descended to earth; its social order and conduct are perpetually unmixed with the impurities of other ages, and it maintains the stability of the Kṛta Yuga.

Its fields are furrowed by ploughs that, because of the abundance of land-lotuses, uproot the lotus-fibers, while the bees, drawn by the excellence of the earth’s essence, raise a tumultuous hum as if singing aloud."
It was densely covered with continuous rows of sugar-cane fields that appeared as if drenched by clouds raining down the water of the ocean of nectar;
its entire borders were crowded with heaps of grain being distributed in every direction like unprecedented mountains, serving as the very abodes of threshing floors;
and its ground was matted with clusters of cumin plants being sprinkled from all sides by upturned water-pots.
It was adorned with rice fields that were increasingly fertile,
and it was occupied by the surfaces of the plains which were variegated by heaps of king-beans crumbling in ripeness,

and which were tawny with the bursting pods of mung beans; and it resounded with the charming tinkling of small bells fastened to the necks of wandering buffaloes, which were tended by singing cowherds and followed by sparrows greedy for swarms of insects.

Its forests were whitened by herds of cattle, which, satisfied with grass that could be cut even by their tears, exuded milk as if it were the Ocean of Milk divided in many ways out of fear that the bull of Śiva might drink it;
its regions were made variegated by black antelopes, as numerous as the thousand eyes of Indra when blinded by the smoke of various sacrificial oblations;

and it was graced by locales made pale by the pollen of *ketakī* groves emitting white smoke, appearing like the very entrances to the city of Śiva, grey with the ashes used for the first ritual smearing.
The surface of the earth near the villages was darkened by the sprouts of *śāka* plants;
at every step, there were rows of young camels who had crushed the shoots of *pīlu* trees, smeared their palms with the juice of tender *mātuluṅga* leaves,

and scattered heaps of flowers made from saffron filaments arranged at will, while travelers— having fallen asleep for the pleasure of drinking the fresh juice of fruits— resembled nectar-distribution halls provided by forest deities.

Its exits were made alluring by groves of pomegranate trees, where the fruit was shimmering within arbors of grapevines, and whose blossoms— reddened by the beaks of parrots clinging to the seeds— were mistaken for the cheeks of swarms of monkeys perched upon them;

it was delightful with pleasure gardens where coconut-liquor was being drunk by forest guards, where clusters of dates were being plundered by travelers, where the sweet-scented juice of *piṇḍīra* fruits was being licked by langurs, and where *āruka* fruits were being pecked at by the beaks of *cakora* birds.
It was filled with forest-fortresses that served as refuges for hundreds of travelers, whose embankments were fouled by herds of cattle descending from Gokula;
it was crowded with camels and lambs being tended by young boys from Karabhīya;

and in every direction, with its mouths upturned and nostrils flared, the earth was smeared with the juice of saffron-pastes trampled by the rolling of horses—evidently to entice the steeds of the Sun’s chariot and to stimulate the speed of the foals lying within their bellies.
It was filled with herds of mares wandering at will like wind-deer that drink as if they were the very wind;
its world was whitened by virtues that proceeded like swarms of swans from the perpetual darkness of sacrificial smoke;
and the realm of living beings was made resonant by riches that were like peacocks intoxicated by the sound of drums in a musical performance.
It was adorned with virtuous men whose circular forms were as white as moonbeams, like pearls set upon a string;
it was to be sought out by all guests, like great trees whose abundant fruits are plucked by hundreds of travelers;
and it was made stable by eminent men covered in deer-hair garments that bore the fragrance of musk, like the foothills of the Himalayas.

There was a country named Śrīkaṇṭha, adorned with lakes that resembled the circle of Nārāyaṇa’s navel, where the best of the twice-born sat upon thousand-petaled lotuses with uplifted stalks; its quarters were filled with great sounds from the churning of waters, which washed the earth as if with streams of milk, like the onset of the churning of the Ocean of Milk;
there, false doctrines perished as if scorched by the water-falls of tears shed by the smoke of the three sacred fires.
Sins were no longer visible, as if burnt away by the fire of the bricks being baked in the sacrificial hearths;
unrighteousness was torn asunder, as if split by axes cutting the wood for the sacrificial posts;
and the confusion of castes vanished, as if washed away by the torrents from the clouds of smoke rising from the flames of the sacrifice.
As if being shattered by the horns of many thousands of cows being given away, Kali fled;
as if cut to pieces by the multitude of chisels from the striking against the stones of the celestial abode, calamities were torn asunder;
and as if pursued by the tumultuous sound of the performance of great gifts, misfortunes ran away.
Diseases dissolved away as if scorched by the fires of thousands of blazing sacrificial hearths;

untimely deaths did not approach, as if terrified by the sharp sound of the holy drums beaten at the marriage of a bull; calamities departed, as if deafened by the continuous chanting of the *brahmaghoṣa*;
and evil fate had no power, as if overcome by the authority of Dharma.
And there, in such a place—delightful with the fragrant scent of flowers from various lovely groves like the very onset of youth for the world;
beautified by many thousands of buffalo-cows dusted with saffron paste like the inner apartments of Dharma;
and its borders whitened by hundreds of yak-tail fans being waved by the breeze like a region of the realm of the gods—;
With the ten horizons blazing from thousands of flaming sacrificial fires, it was like the encampment of the Kṛta Yuga;
with all misfortune being quelled through the meditations of Brahman-sages seated upon lotus-thrones, it was like the first descent of the world of Brahmā;
and crowded with hundreds of great rivers resounding with clamor, it was like the adversary of the inhabitants of Uttarakuru.
With all its people unacquainted with the torments of seeking wealth from kings, it was like a conqueror of Tripura;

white with rows of palatial buildings whitened by the essence of nectar, it was like a counterpart to the world of the moon; and filling the earth with the sound of ornaments from women intoxicated by the wine of spring, it was like a rival to the city of Kubera.
The specific region called Sthāṇvīśvara was known as a "grove of asceticism" by sages, and as a "sanctuary of love" by courtesans.
It was regarded as a hall of music by dancers, a city of Yama by enemies, a ground of wish-fulfilling gems by supplicants, and a field of heroes by those who live by the sword.
It is called "the preceptor’s household" by students,
"a city of Gandharvas" by singers,
and "the workshop of Viśvakarman" by those possessed of specialized knowledge.
To those who pay homage, it is the "ground of gain";
to gamblers, the "place of play";
and to the virtuous, the "assembly of the good."
It is called the "Vajra-enclosure" by those who have sought refuge; the "assembly of connoisseurs" by the refined; and the "fruition of good deeds" by travelers.
It was called "the cave of the Asuras" by the logicians, "the hermitage of the Śākyas" by the ascetics, "the city of the Apsarases" by the lovers,
and "a great festive assembly" by the bards.
And it was called Vasudhārā by the brahmins;
for therein were women who walked like elephants yet possessed virtuous character, and those who were fair-complexioned yet devoted to wealth.
They were pale yet flushed with passion; their faces were as pure as white lotuses, yet their breath was fragrant with wine;
their bodies possessed the luster of moonstones, yet their limbs were as tender as the *śirīṣa* flower.
They were inaccessible to libertines yet wore bodices; they possessed the splendor of many wives yet were joined with impoverished husbands;
they were full of loveliness and sweet-spoken.
There, the women were vigilant, their facial complexions radiant with clarity, free from affectation, and mature;
for these women, their very eyes were the natural ornament of a garland of severed heads, while garlands of blue lotus petals were a mere burden;
the reflections of their curls upon the surface of their broad foreheads served as unartificial ear-ornaments, making the fresh sprouts of the *tamāla* tree redundant.

Only pleasant conversation is the auspicious ornament for the ears, whereas earrings and the like are mere ostentation; the cheeks themselves are the constant source of light, while jeweled lamps at night are but a display of wealth; the swarm of bees attracted by fragrant breath is the lovely veil for the face, whereas the custom of noble women to wear a net-veil is merely a burden; and speech itself is the most melodious lute, while external knowledge and the striking of strings are but superficial learning.

Her laughter alone is exceedingly fragrant; camphor dust is useless as a perfumed powder. The radiance of her lower lip alone is a more brilliant cosmetic; saffron paste is a meritless stain upon her loveliness.
Her arms alone are most tender.

The cane-sticks used for playful blows were as useless as lotus stalks; the drops of sweat from the heat of youth were the only true ornaments for the breasts, while pearl necklaces were merely burdens;
the hips themselves, broad and square like surfaces of great crystal slabs, were the cause of rest for those filled with passion, whereas the jeweled terraces of the palace were without purpose.
The buzzing swarms of bees upon the lotus-stalk bracelets served as his resonant foot-ornaments, rendering the sapphire anklets useless;
the domestic kalahaṃsa geese, drawn by the sound of the anklets, were his only fitting companions for walking—such was the manifestation of his sovereignty, with his attendants as his retinue.
And there, like the thousand-eyed Indra in person, he bore a bow that displayed every hue.
He was like Mount Meru in his auspicious nature,
like Mount Mandara in attracting prosperity,
and like the ocean in his adherence to the bounds of propriety.
He was as if composed of space at the manifestation of sound,
as if composed of the moon in the gathering of its digits,
and as if composed of the Vedas in his unartificial eloquence.
Like the earth itself in supporting the world,
like the wind itself in removing all the dust and impurities of kings,
he was a preceptor in speech.
Pṛthu in his chest, Viśāla in his mind,
Janaka in his asceticism.
Suyātra in matters of splendor, Sumantra in private counsel, and Budha in the assembly;
Arjuna in fame, Bhīṣma in archery, and Niṣadha in physical form.

There was a king named Puṣyabhūti, who was a slayer of enemies in battle, a hero, one who had subdued the Śūrasenas, and who was intent upon the welfare of his subjects; he appeared as if fashioned from the massed splendor of all the primordial kings.
"This Gaurīvega was created by Pṛthu," said he who, as if in rivalry, made the great earth his queen;
for the mind of the great is naturally independent and follows its own inclination,
since his devotion to the Blessed One, untaught by anyone, was innate from childhood and directed toward no other deity.
O fragrant with devotion,
sustainer of the world,
creator of all beings!
For one whose existence was being severed,
devotion to Bhava became even greater;
without performing the ritual worship of the Bull-bannered Lord, he did not take food even in his dreams.
The unborn, the undecaying,
the teacher of the immortals,
the enemy of the city of the asuras.
to Gaṇapati, who is not surpassed by any,
the husband of the daughter of the mountain,
to whom all the worlds have performed prostrations at his feet;
Having taken refuge in Paśupati, he saw the three worlds as devoid of any other deity;
for the natures of dependents follow the mind of their master.
Thus, indeed, the Blessed Lord who wields the broken axe was worshipped in every house.

In that holy land, winds blew, laden with the fragrance of abundant guggulu resin melting in the fires of the sacrificial hearths, scattering droplets from the milk used for ritual ablutions, and wafting the scent of garlands made of *bilva* leaves. The citizens, the attendants at his feet, the ministers, and the great feudal lords—conquered by the strength of his own arm and reduced to tributaries—served him with offerings and gifts appropriate for the worship of Śiva. Indeed, they were present with great silk cloths white as the peaks of Mount Kailāsa, their tips adorned with golden leaf-patterns; with lamps on staffs of precious gems; and with sacred threads.
The ladies of the inner apartments also brought satisfaction to his heart with mouth-covers inlaid with fragments of highly precious rubies;

they themselves began the pounding of rice for the sacrificial offerings, their sprout-like hands became even redder from smearing the temple floors, and their entire retinue was occupied with stringing flowers, thus attending to his every desire.
Furthermore, that king, a supreme devotee of Maheśvara, heard from the people that on earth there lived another holy being who was like the Destroyer of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice incarnate.

The mortal world was filled with thousands of disciples from the South, renowned for their qualities and the power of their manifold sciences, like followers of the great Śaiva master named Bhairavācārya;
for it is the correspondence of character that draws even an unseen person to one's heart.
For as soon as he heard [the news], the king conceived a profound devotion toward that venerable teacher Bhairava, even though he had gone far away like a second Śiva;
and he longed for a vision of him in every way, even in his dreams.
Then one day, when the day was spent and touching the western mountain, the female doorkeeper approached the king in the inner apartments and announced: “O Lord!”
A wandering mendicant stood at the gate and said,
"By the word of Bhairavācārya, I have arrived before Your Majesty. Upon hearing this, the king respectfully asked, "Where is he?"
"Bring him right here; let him enter," he said,
and the female doorkeeper did accordingly.
And before long, he saw approaching a tall man with arms reaching to his knees, who, though emaciated from living on alms, appeared as if stout due to his thick-boned limbs.
He had a broad head, a forehead with prominent folds and deep depressions, and hollow cheeks devoid of flesh.
His eyes were tawny like drops of honey and perfectly round; his eyebrows were slightly arched; and one of his ear-lobes hung down extremely long.
With rows of teeth as formidable and prominent as gourd seeds,
with lower lips as slack as the necks of horses,
and with long faces and pendulous chins;
He wore a saffron-colored yogapaṭṭaka draped over his shoulder as a *vaikakṣaka* (cross-shoulder cloth);

he had fashioned an upper garment (*uttarāsaṅga*) from a piece of rag, reddened by mineral pigments and knotted at the center of his chest as if it were passion torn into fragments; and he carried a broom made of bamboo strips for cleaning clay, its handle fixed steady by being wrapped with a double layer of young grass, its top-end provided with a loincloth.

His shoulder was supported by a yogic staff (*yogabhāraka*) held in his left hand, which contained an alms-bowl (*bhikṣākapālaka*) nestled within a pouch made from a date-palm leaf; it featured a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) fixed upon three wooden planks arranged in a triangle with three handles, and it provided a place for sandals that had been fashioned in various ways, while a bundle of books tied with thick cords hung from it.
He saw a wandering mendicant holding a cane seat in his other hand;
the lord of the earth also immediately favored him with appropriate respect.
And as he sat down, the king asked: "Where is Bhairavācārya?"

His mind delighted by the respectful words of the king, the wandering mendicant informed him that [the sage] was staying in a deserted monastery situated in a grove on the bank of the Sarasvatī near the city.

He further spoke: “The Blessed One honors the illustrious one with words of blessing,” and having said this, he drew from his ascetic’s staff-bag five jeweled objects sent by Bhairavācārya, which illuminated the interior of the palace with their intense radiance.
The lotuses were made of silver.

But the king, fearing to break the affection of his dear friend, yet constrained by courtesy and unable to disregard the propriety of accepting such a gift, remained for a long time with a wavering mind; finally, overcome by his great goodness, he accepted them with great difficulty.
And he said: "This devotion to Śiva, the cause of the production of all fruits, bears us fruits that are difficult even for our desires to attain;
for by this, the venerable Bhairavācārya, the teacher of the world, is so pleased with us.
Tomorrow I shall see the Blessed One. Having spoken thus, he dismissed the mendicant.
And by this news, he attained supreme joy.
On the following day, rising early at dawn, he mounted his horse, with a white parasol raised aloft and a pair of white chowries being waved;
surrounded by only a few princes, he set out to see Bhairavācārya, as the moon sets out to see the sun.
Having gone a short distance, he saw one of that master's disciples approaching him from the opposite direction.
He asked, "Where does the Blessed One reside?
The disciple replied, "He resides in the middle of the bilva grove to the north of this ruined mother-temple."
Having gone to that place, he dismounted from his horse and entered the grove of *bilva* trees. Then,
in the midst of a great multitude of wandering mendicants (*kārpaṭika*), he was already bathed in the early morning.
Having performed his morning ablutions and offered the oblations to the fire,
he sat upon a tiger skin spread over the ground smeared with green cow-dung, having already cleared the area around him by drawing lines of ashes.
He appeared as if practicing a dwelling in the darkness of Pātāla out of fear of entering the caverns of the Asuras, under the guise of his black woolen cloak;
with the tawny luster of his own radiance, like a flash of lightning, he seemed to smear his circle of disciples with red arsenic paste purchased for the sale of "great flesh";
and with his topknot tied upward, from which hung Rudrākṣa beads and conch-shell counters from one side, he seemed to bind them fast.
He was wandering about as a perfected one (siddha), arrogant and conceited due to his learning;
though his age exceeded fifty years by a few white hairs on his head, there remained only a few strands of hair on his scalp, which were thinning due to baldness.
With ears covered in hair and a broad forehead,
he produced, by means of many oblique lines of ash, a streak as white as the skull-bone cracked open by the heat of the thick *guggulu* resin applied repeatedly to his head.
He bore a single, long, unbroken line of brows that appeared as one due to their meeting at the center, with the portion of his beard contracted by the folds of the natural wrinkles on his forehead;

with his pair of exceedingly long eyes— whose pupils were like shimmering glass, whose red outer corners emitted a spreading mass of rays, and which possessed a rainbow-like luster in their dark centers— he seemed to paint a great circle of many-colored tints all around him, while a multitude of white, yellow, and red banners fluttered about him.
Scattering lines of flame like those of Śiva’s fire in all directions,
with the tip of his nose curved by the point of Tārkṣya’s beak,
and with his cheeks drawn inward by his widely gaped corners of the mouth;
He was whitening the quarters of the sky with the light of his teeth, which issued forth as if from the moonlight of the crescent moon resting upon his heart;
his lips were slightly protruding as if from the excessive weight of all the *Śaiva-saṃhitās* resting upon his tongue;

and he was being bound by the two crystal earrings swinging from the lobes of his long ears, like Śukra and Bṛhaspati being drawn along by their faith in the mastery of the sciences for conquering gods and demons.

With his right hand, he was whirling a rosary of rudrākṣa beads— which resembled a row of buckets on a water-lifting wheel for drawing from the well of all aesthetic sentiments— and which had been made into an ornament out of devotion by the Blessed Lord Śiva when he shattered the frontal bone of Pūṣan, as if it were a section of the sun’s teeth, bound together by a string of medicinal herbs and mantras;
while with a mass of matted locks, the tips of which were tawny and dangling upon his chest, he seemed to be sweeping away the internal dust of his own passions.

He possessed a region of the heart that was covered with an extremely dense circle of blue hair and seemed as if scorched by the light obtained through meditation; his belly was being bound by a waistband of slightly loosened folds, and the masses of flesh on his buttocks were becoming diminished.
He wore a white sacred thread and a linen loincloth;

his body was encircled by a yogic cloth as white as the foam of nectar, which, with its firm cross-legged posture, seemed like the serpent Vāsuki being circumambulated by him as he manifested the power of countless unimpeded mantras.

With the stainless lattice of rays from the nails of his pair of feet—whose soles were exceedingly delicate due to the weight of their ruddy hue—he seemed to shatter the depths of the underworld (rasātala) through his passion for uprooting great treasures.

He was resplendent with a pair of cool sandals, washed clean with water, which reached as high as his ankles like a pair of swans that had come along from their familiarity with pilgrimages to the banks of the Bhagirathi;

he shone with a bamboo staff topped with a crooked iron spike driven into its end, which stood constantly by his side like a goad for removing the Vinayakas who obstruct the attainment of all branches of knowledge;
he spoke little, smiled gently, was helpful to all, and observed the vow of celibacy from his youth.
One who is exceedingly ascetic,
highly magnanimous, free from anger, and not lacking in devotion.
It was adorned by its noble nature like a great city;
it possessed a delicate luster from the mass of excellent garments like the Kalpa-trees upon Mount Meru;
and its summit was purified by the dust from the feet of Paśupati, like Mount Kailāsa.
It was like the world of Śiva, followed by the hosts of Maheśvara’s attendants;
like the ocean, its body washed by thousands of various rivers and streams;
and like the flow of the Gaṅgā, pure with many holy bathing places.
The abode of Dharma, the ford of truth, and the treasury of virtue.
A city of purity, a hall of good conduct,
a field of forbearance, a rice-field of modesty,
and a city of sanctity.
She is the hall of good character,
the field of forbearance, the abode of modesty,
and the place of steadfastness.
The support of fortitude, the mine of compassion,
the abode of curiosity,
and the garden of loveliness.
A palace of serenity,
a home of reverence,
and a social gathering of kindness.
He beheld Bhairavācārya, who was like the Lord Virūpākṣa incarnate, the source of all existence and the very embodiment of the Kali age.
But Bhairavācārya, seeing the king from afar, stirred like the ocean at the sight of the moon;
his circle of disciples, rising even before him, stood up and went forward to meet him.
Offering a *śrīphala* fruit as a gift, he uttered a blessing with a voice as deep as the pool from which the stream of the Ganges was being disgorged by Jahnu’s ear.
The king also, with eyes whose whiteness was expanded by joy as if returning a multitude of lotus groves, and displaying— as it were—

the favor of Maheśvara through the emergence of a third eye in the form of his crest-jewel which was dripping from his broad forehead, performed a fresh salutation while bowing low from afar; he was like one being released from every last fragment of sin uprooted by service to Śiva, for bees were fleeing from his drooping ear-lobes.

The teacher also said, "Come, sit here," and displayed his own tiger-skin seat. Having shown such courtesy, the king spoke these words, which were as sweet as the season of spring and as charming as the faltering voice of an intoxicated swan, like the flow of a great river: "Venerable sir, you ought not to rebuke me for the lapses of other kings."

"This is surely a transgression of character or a wickedness of fortune on the part of my elder, who acts thus toward me—me who am disregarded by all kings and whose prosperity has been destroyed. This is no ground for such formalities; enough with this excessive constraint."
"Even though he stands at a distance, this person is a disciple of your heart's desire;
and the seat of a guru, which is worthy of honor like a teacher himself, ought not to be bypassed.
May you yourselves sit here," he said, and having spoken thus, he sat down upon a garment brought by his attendants.
Bhairavācārya, too, complying with the king’s command which could not be disregarded out of affection, resumed that very tiger skin as before.
When the royal retinue and the circle of disciples were seated, he offered them the appropriate guest-offering (*arghya*) and other honors.

Then, his heart captivated by the king’s sweetness, he spoke—manifesting, as it were, his devotion to Śiva in the form of shimmering rays from his teeth, pure like a mass of moonbeams: “My dear sir, [The rest of the passage continues with the teacher's speech.]**
Your extreme humility itself proclaims the weight of your virtues;
you are a vessel for every excellence,
yet your conduct is proportionate to your wealth.
From birth, I have indeed cast no glance upon my own possessions;
for there exists a body somewhere that has not been sold for wealth— which is but fuel for the fire of the entire multitude of vices—
and there are vital breaths preserved by means of alms.
There are a few syllables of knowledge that have been poorly grasped;
however, there are also some small fragments of merit acquired through service at the feet of the venerable Lord Śiva, which remain close at hand.
Please accept whatever among these is fit for use here.
"For the minds of the virtuous are like flowers, to be grasped only by those with very delicate fibers.
Moreover, O dear one, the righteous, esteemed by the wise, produce fame even in a most callous heart, just as well-known words do upon being heard.
I have been brought here by this auspicious youth, carried away by the streams of his multitude of virtues, like foam-white waves entering a cavern and being swept along by curiosity."
The king, however, replied to him: "Venerable sir, even regarding one's own body and such, for the virtuous, masters alone are the beloved ones.
Furthermore, an immeasurable mass of merit has already been acquired simply by the sight of you."
"By this very arrival, I have been raised to a desirable station by my teacher," he said, and after staying for a long time with various conversations, he went home.
On another day, Bhairavācārya also went to see the king;
and the king offered himself to him along with his harem, his retinue, and his treasury.
And he, smiling, said: "Father,
where are riches,
and where are we, raised in the forest?"
"Noble-mindedness withers completely under the heat of wealth like a creeper;
our kind of spiritedness, which does not oppress others, shines like that of fireflies.
Only those such as yourself are the proper vessels for prosperity. Having said this, he stood for a short while and then departed.
The wandering mendicant, in that same manner, presented five silver lotuses as gifts at each turn.
On one occasion, however, he entered carrying something wrapped in a white cloth;
having sat down and remained for a moment as before, he said: "O illustrious one!"
"The Blessed One has said to you that there is a Brahmin named Pātālasvāmin who is my disciple;
by him, the great sword named Aṭṭahāsa was recovered from the hand of a Brahma-rākṣasa.
This very sword is worthy of your arm; please take it. Having spoken thus, he drew it from its covering of tattered rags—like the expanse of the autumn sky condensed into a single mass.
Like the stream of the Kālindī with its waters solidified;
like the serpent Kāliya, enraged at Kṛṣṇa out of a desire to conquer his sword Nandaka, yet having become an object of compassion;
like a fragment of a cloud from the dissolution of the world fallen from the sky, manifesting a torrential downpour for the destruction of the world.
With its visible circle of formidable fangs, it was like the very laughter of violence;
it was like the staff-like arm of Hari, with a firmly clenched fist;
and it seemed as if it were fashioned from the Kālakūṭa poison, capable of snatching away the life-force of the entire world.
It was as if forged from iron heated by the fire of the wrath of Kṛtānta;

owing to its extreme sharpness, it seemed to shriek even at the touch of the wind as if in anger, and by the reflection falling upon the jeweled floor of the assembly hall, it appeared to split itself in two with a *caṭacaṭa* sound;
its edge was made formidable by rays of light that resembled hair clinging to it after the severing of an enemy's head.
With flashes of lightning flickering again and again, its circle of radiance scattered the heat of the sun,
as if cutting the day into fragments,
like a sidelong glance from the Night of Doom.
Like an ear-lotus of Time,
like the syllable *oṃ* of Cruelty, an ornament of Egoism, and a family friend of Anger.
The body of pride,
the companion of recklessness,
and the offspring of death.
It was the path for the arrival of fortune and the path for the departure of fame— the sword.
The king, having taken it in his hand, looked at it for a long time as if embracing it with his arm out of love for his weapon, under the guise of measuring its length.

And he sent this message: "The Blessed One should be told: 'Though my mind is ill-disposed by its contempt for seizing the property of others, it is nonetheless unable to commit the transgression of violating your word.
But the wandering mendicant, being well-pleased that the object had been accepted, said: "May it be well with you."
Having said, "We shall accomplish it," he departed.
The king, who by nature was a lover of the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*), considered the earth to be already within the palm of his hand because of that sword.
Then, as the days passed, on one occasion Bhairavācārya approached the king and spoke to him with courtesy: "My dear sir!"
The dispositions of the fortunate are such that they are indifferent to their own interests yet skillful in helping others;

for those like you, the sight of a petitioner is a great festival, and to receive him, to honor him, to accept his request, and to assist him is a source of joy. You are the ground upon which the desires of all the world rest.
By which you are addressed:
listen.

I have already performed the preliminary service for ten million recitations in a great cremation ground, according to the ritual manual, for the Great Mantra named the Heart of the Blessed One Mahākāla, wearing black garlands, garments, and ointments as prescribed by the ritual.
And his success culminates in the accomplishment of a vetāla;
that is difficult to attain without companions,
and you are sufficient for this task.
And when you have taken up the burden, there will be three other companions:
one is that very same maskarin named Ṭāṭibha, our childhood friend, who attends upon you;
the second is that Pātālasvāmin.
"Furthermore, there is another disciple of mine, a Dravidian named Kaṇatāla;
if you think it right, then let this arm of mine—long as the trunk of an elephant of the quarters, grasping the Aṭṭahāsa sword—be taken for one night as a bolt for the gate of a single direction.

When he had spoken thus, the King, who was like one who has entered darkness and suddenly beheld light, his spirit uplifted by having obtained such assistance, replied with a joyful heart: "O Blessed One!"

"I am most highly favored by this command, which is common to all your disciples; I feel as though my very self has been taken under your protection," said Bhairavācārya, and he rejoiced at those words spoken by the king.

He then made an appointment: "On this coming fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, at this very hour, you, sir, accompanied by a companion bearing a weapon, must go to that deserted temple situated near the great cemetery."
"We must be seen," he thought.
Then, after several days had passed, on that very fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the king was initiated according to the Śaiva rite and undertook his religious observances.
He then consecrated the sword Aṭṭahāsa, having performed its preliminary consecration (adhivāsa) and offered it worship with perfumes, incense, garlands, and other offerings.

Then, as the day drew to a close, when the quarters of the sky were turning crimson as if some had offered blood-sacrifices for the sake of performing rites, and when the rays of the sun hung down like the tongues of night-prowlers greedy for offerings of blood;
and while the sun, having taken up the western quarter through its affection for the king, seemed itself to desire to assume the office of a world-guardian (dikpāla).
While the shadows of the trees grew as if among female sorceresses, while masses of darkness rose like Dānavas dwelling in the depths of Pātāla to create obstacles,
and while the host of stars gathered in the sky as if desiring to witness a fierce deed, the night became profound.

In the dead of night, when all people were asleep and the world was hushed in silence, the king, having deceived his inner apartments and attendants, took up the sword Aṭṭahāsa with his right hand— its hilt shimmering in his left— and,

with the spreading mass of light from the blade veiling his entire body as if with a cloak of blue silk out of fear of being seen, he proceeded, followed by an escort who followed him even though they had not been commanded.
As if drawing royal fortune after him by the guise of swarms of bees clinging to his fragrance, he departed from the city alone, as though pulling success toward himself by its hair;
and he went to that place.
Then those three also approached him, like Aśvatthāman, Kṛpa, and Kṛtavarman, fully armed for a night-attack, bathed, wearing garlands, and having assumed formidable disguises.

With bees hovering over their flower-crests and humming as if performing the binding of the sacrificial tufts (*mantra-śikhā-bandha*), they bore upon their heads turbans that displayed formidable *svastika* knots formed at the center of the forehead, appearing like the binding of great mudrās (*mahāmudrā-bandha*).

With faces whose cheeks were whitened by the spreading luster of pure ivory ear-ornaments extending from one ear-opening, they seemed to drink in the nocturnal darkness, desiring to diminish the power of the night-stalkers.
Their limbs were anointed as if with pure, mantra-consecrated *gorocanā* by the brilliant luster of jeweled earrings hanging from their other ears;

they brandished sharp swords that seemed to offer human sacrifices for the sake of ritual success, bearing within them their own reflections, while the spreading boundaries of the rays from those swords appeared to divide the night into three parts, as if to protect each of their respective quarters of the sky.

Tearing [the enemy] apart with crescent-headed arrows, they held shields that resembled the night— studded with clusters of shimmering stars like bubbles of silver— and thus created another unseasonable night;
their bows were rendered motionless by being tightly bound with sets of golden chains.
With their swords girded, Ṭīṭibha, Karṇatāla, and Pātālasvāmin announced themselves;
and the king asked, "Who is here? Who?"
Thus he questioned the three; and all three of them announced their respective names.
Followed by them alone, he proceeded toward that place where the quarters of the sky were seized by the smoke of guggulu incense, worn thin by the world, yet thick with the lamps offered to Bali.

The site for the ritual practice was prepared with all necessary implements; it was silent, profound, and terrifying, where darkness seemed to flee as if scorched by the half-burnt protective mustard seeds being scattered about.
In the center of a great mandala drawn there with ash white as the pollen of night-lotuses stood one whose radiance spread with even more intense brilliance.
He was like the autumnal sun encircled by a broad halo,
or like Mount Mandara situated within the whirlpool of the churning Ocean of Milk;

he sat upon the chest of a corpse lying supine, smeared with red sandalwood paste and adorned with red garlands, garments, and ornaments, and had begun a fire-ritual in the cavity of its mouth where a fire had been kindled.
He has a black turban, black body-unguent, and a black protective cord.
Clad in black garments,
he seemed, under the guise of offerings of black sesame seeds, to be bringing to destruction the atoms of impurity that cause the human condition, out of a thirst for the state of a Vidyādhara;
with the rays of his fingernails, he appeared to be washing the fire-god— who had been defiled by contact with the mouths of the hungry ghosts— after it was overturned by the pouring of oblations.
With eyes red as smoke, he seemed to be casting an offering of blood into the fire;
with his mouth, from which the tips of his white teeth were visible through slightly parted lips, he appeared to be muttering some mantra, its syllables clearly manifest;
and by means of the nearby lamps reflected in the sweat of his exertion from the *homa*, he seemed to be burning all his limbs for the sake of the ritual’s success.
He saw the Bhairavācārya, encircled by a sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) draped over his shoulder with many strands, like a sovereign spell-king (*vidyārāja*);
having approached, he paid homage,
and being welcomed by him, he attended to his own duties.
In the meantime, Pātālasvāmī took possession of the eastern quarter belonging to Indra;
Karṇatāla, the wandering mendicant, [took] the northern quarter belonging to Kubera;
and the king adorned the direction marked by the light of Triśaṅku’s son.

While the guardians of the quarters remained thus stationed, and while the Bhairava-ācārya— having entered the cage of the guardians' arms— was fearlessly accomplishing his rite, and while the obstructing demons (kauṇapa) had long raised a clamor only to find their efforts fruitless and were now silenced;
at a time when midnight was passing, suddenly, not far to the north of the mandala...
The earth split open, displaying what seemed like the hollow of the tusk of the Great Boar at the time of universal dissolution;
and from that very fissure, as if an iron pillar for tethering the elephants of the quarters had been uprooted,
there emerged one whose broad shoulders were like those of the Great Boar, who rose from the womb of the earth like the demon Naraka, and burst forth from the netherworld like the Dānava Bali.
Like a sapphire palace with jewel-lamps blazing above,

he possessed a beautiful head crowned by glossy, dark, thick, and curly locks of hair, and wore a blooming garland of *mālatī* flowers; with a faltering voice and naturally rosy eyes, he appeared as if intoxicated by the pride of youth, his neck-garlands swaying and slipping.

Repeatedly smearing the peaks of his shoulders— which resembled the frontal globes of the elephants of the quarters— with clay kneaded in his cupped hands, he appeared like a portion of the autumnal sky streaked with fragments of dense white clouds by means of thick sandalwood paste applied as irregular patches;
and with his waist further attenuated by a *caṇḍātaka* garment as pale as the inner leaf of a *ketakī* flower.
Having assumed a formal posture, with the end of his white exercise-cloth— fluttering in his playful movements— held behind him as if by a serpent resting upon the ground, he,

whose thighs were firm and thick like pillars, set down his slow steps as if out of fear of breaking the earth, and with difficulty, as though carrying a mountain, moved with a gait heavy with intense pride.
Lifting his body with pride, repeatedly doubling his left arm across his chest while tossing his right leg sideways and curling his lower leg,

that man— dark as a blue lotus— emerged, making the world of living beings seem as if deprived of its senses with the loud *ṭāṅkāra* sounds of his fierce slapping, striking blows like thunderclaps that deafened the ears; and laughing, he spoke with a voice as terrible as the roar of Narasiṃha.

Bhāratī said: "O Vidyādhara, you who lust after the unworthy! Is this pride in your learning or intoxication with your companionship that, like a fool, you desire success from this man without first offering him a sacrifice? What kind of evil thought is this of yours?"
In all this time, has the lord of this land—the one by whose very name this country is designated—never reached the vicinity of your ears as I, the Naga named Śrīkaṇṭha?
While I am unwilling, what power do you have even to seize me, let alone travel through the sky?
And yet, this protector of the earth is himself helpless, a wretched man who is being treated as a mere tool by base followers of Śiva such as yourself.

"Now, endure the fruit of this wicked conduct along with this evil king! Having spoken thus, he struck down all three—Tīṭibha and the others—with cruel blows from his forearms as they rushed toward him, sending them to their deaths along with their bodies, armor, and swords.

Then, upon hearing such unprecedented insults, even though they were unarmed and unwounded, they seemed to vomit forth the water of sword-blades drunk during many battles under the guise of the sweat of indignation.
Even with their limbs bristling as if with horripilation, they made themselves light— as if to spring forth for battle— by shedding the burden of the multitude of arrow-heads;

and even with their loud laughter, which reflected the clusters of stars and clearly revealed rows of white teeth as if mocking the enemy, they proclaimed their own steadfastness through the circle of rays from their fingernails, whirled about by the shifting movements of their girded arms.

Preventing the ten directions with the binding of a mantra-circle for subduing serpents, as if fearing his departure, the lord of men spoke with contempt: "O crow, you who have the belly of a serpent!
While I, the royal swan, remain present, do you not feel shame in begging for an offering?
What is the use of these harsh words?"
Valor resides in the arm, not in speech;
take up a weapon!
You shall not remain alive.
"My arm is untrained to strike those who have not grasped a weapon," said the Naga, treating him with even greater contempt: "Come!
What need is there for a weapon?"
"I shall shatter your pride with my very arms!"—having spoken thus, he slapped his limbs.
The king, too, feeling ashamed to conquer one unarmed with a weapon in battle, cast aside his sword Aṭṭahāsa along with its shield and leather guard, and girded his loins for a wrestling match.
And the two fought, drenched by sprays of blood from their arms split by merciless slapping, making the world seem as if composed of sound alone with their falling, pillar-like arms.
Before long, the king threw the serpent to the ground,
seized him by the hair,
and drew his sword Aṭṭahāsa to cut off his head.

And he saw his sacred thread through the garland worn across his shoulder; then, having ceased his activity with weapons, he said: "O ill-behaved one! This is the seed for you to carry out your wicked conduct."
"Since you act with such confidence in your own restlessness," he said, and then released him.
Immediately thereafter, he suddenly beheld an exceedingly thick moonlight;
and he smelled a fragrance, intoxicating to the sense of smell, like that of lotus groves blooming in autumn.
Instantly he heard the sound of anklets and directed his gaze along the path of that sound. Then,
in the midst of the *Aṭṭahāsa* sword held in his palm, he saw her flashing like lightning within the belly of a dark cloud, as if drinking up the night with her radiance.
She held a lotus in her hand,
and as she drew her feet along, the networks of lines from the glow of her tender fingers seemed like a forest of young coral creepers clinging to the shore;
out of fear that the moon’s orb might close its lotus-like hands, she bore it, as it were, in fragments under the guise of the multitude of her spotless toe-nails.
She appeared as if she had descended after slipping from the firm binding of her girdle due to the weight of the anklets resting upon her ankles;

she seemed to be emerging from the waters of the ocean through her exceedingly transparent garment, which was stirred by the wind into slender ripples and adorned with hundreds of various flowers and birds;
and her waist was embraced by the triple-pathed Ganges under the guise of her three folds, out of love for her birth in the ocean.
She possessed a circle of breasts so exceedingly high that she resembled a quarter of the sky where the frontal globes of the world-elephants were visible;
